title: Chess for refugee children: A winning move
summary: As champions gather at the World Chess Olympiad in Uzbekistan an inspirational initiative is changing the lives of traumatised youngsters Chess might seem an unlikely game-changer to transform the lives of refugee children. But that’s exactly what is causing a buzz for youngsters living in the harshest conditions across Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, the largest refugee camp in the world. And the move is backed by the International Chess Federation (FIDE), the Himalayan Chess Academy, and a national women’s champion. In camp an excited group of children gather around a one US dollar chess set, eyes fixed in anticipation of a girl with her finger resting on the small white piece in contemplation of her next move. Check! Some gasp; some giggle. But the focus, the tension, and the sense of engagement are tangible. It’s a scene repeated on a dozen chess boards under the makeshift roofing of a refugee community space. And it’s changing lives. Magnus Wolfe-Murray smiles as he watches. The charismatic Scot, a seasoned aid worker, has brought the game into the lives of the Rohingya communities with his grass roots charity Movement in Refuge. It’s not all about chess. It’s about play, movement, activity and engagement, including sports like roundnet and football. He’s just beginning. Yet introducing the ‘Chess for Protection Programme’ in August in partnership with FIDE has been a winning move. Wolfe-Murray said: “The impact of introducing chess to youngsters in the camp has been amazing. With a few chess sets and some coaching! The game is a great focus. The engagement and genuine excitement we have been able to achieve has been brilliant. It brings with it a confidence and sense of empowerment among the children – we see a real difference. A sense of hope. And lots of smiles. “Now we’re hoping we can raise funds to extend our activities to include many more of the thousands of children across the camps, working with and training additional coaches from within the refugee community,” he adds. Beside him stands Monalisha Khamboo, the first women’s chess champion of Nepal, who received the distinction of the Woman Candidate Master title from FIDE in 2015. The game transformed her own life from a shy girl in a poor village in Eastern Nepal, hindered by a serious stammer, teased by peers and teachers alike. Chess changed her trajectory completely; she earned a sport scholarship through chess to gain a place at a high school in Kathmandu, and the rest is history. Now she spends her time championing the game across international borders. She’s known Wolfe-Murray from his aid work in Nepal and was happy to help bring the game to refugee children and provide professional coaching. Ms Khamboo commented: “This project is close to my heart. Chess can be an agent of change for every individual, which is what happened to me. From my own personal experience chess can help you build self-esteem; the resilience that comes in the healing journey. Chess is a strong social tool for promoting and working in the Rohingya camps. “We now have thirty chess trainers, so we are on the right path. We can make a better world for living through the game of chess. I am so grateful to FIDE for this opportunity to come and serve here and work with the Rohingya people.” The idea is to bring chess and its benefits to more refugee youngsters in Cox’s Bazar, where there are an estimated 540,000 children according to Government of Bangladesh and United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) numbers. That’s why Wolfe-Murray is attending the World Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, organised by FIDE from 15 to 27 September, 2026, set to draw the world’s chess elite to battle it out in competition. Movement in Refuge hopes to raise additional funding from across the chess community and beyond to reach thousands of youngsters across the 33 camps that make up Cox’s Bazar. And spread the age-old magic of chess. Through partnership, through business, civil society, government… and chess lovers the world over. For more details and/or an interview with Magnus Wolfe-Murray, please contact Andrew Goss on +44 7914 173116; or mail at andy.goss@hotmail.co.uk About Movement in Refuge Movement in Refuge is a grassroots charity established to bring play, movement, and activity to the Rohingya children of Cox’s Bazar, working directly with the refugee community. MiR is a registered charity in Scotland as well as in the USA as a 501.c.3 non-profit organisation. Website: https://www.movementinrefuge.org/ The Programme: The Chess Protection Programme in partnership with FIDE and the Himalayan Chess Academy took place in Kutupalong Refugee Camp during August. It was delivered by FIDE chess instructor and women’s champion MonalishaKhamboo through MiR and local partner The Humanitarian Assistance Programme (HAP/Bangladesh). Thirty chess players took part in coaching sessions and the programme concluded with a girls and boys tournament of 64 refugees aged 10 to 22 years. Funding target: Movement in Refuge hopes to raise USD $100,000 to help bring chess to up to 5,000 more refugee youngsters over the next two years. Refugee numbers: 1,3 million Rohingya are living in the 33 camps that make up Cox’s Bazar, the largest refugee camp in the world. Of those more than 540,000 are children according to the Government of Bangladesh and the UNHCR (as of March, 2025).

title: GCL 2026, Day 7: Ganges Grandmasters crush CheQ Mumba Masters; Alpine APL Pipers defeat FYERS American Gambits to close in on final berth
summary: Ganges Grandmasters and the Pipers will advance to the final if they win their last round robin match on Saturday Ganges Grandmasters and defending champions Alpine APL Pipers registered convincing victories on the penultimate day of the preliminary stage of the Global Chess League (GCL), a joint initiative of Tech Mahindra and FIDE, in Bengaluru on Friday. Both teams need to just win their respective final round matches to secure their spots in the Season 4 title clash. The Pipers defeated the Gambits 9-7 while the Grandmasters thrashed the Mumba Masters 16-1 to post the biggest win of the tournament. In the opening match of the day, Triveni Continental Kings defeated PBG Alaskan Knights 13-7. Both Ganges Grandmasters and Alpine APL Pipers now have 18 match points but the former’s dominant win means that they took the top spot in the overall standings due to better game score. FYERS American Gambits are in third place with 15 match points and would need one of the top two leaders to lose in the final round, while they will have to beat CheQ Mumba Masters by a convincing margin. The Gambits found themselves in this position, as they could not find a way to stop the Pipers in the second match of the day. Let’s take a closer look at today’s matches: PBG Alaskan Knights vs Triveni Continental Kings: 7-13 In the match between two bottom-placed teams, two-time champions Triveni Continental Kings proved too strong for the PBG Alaskan Knights. On the Superstar women boards, Zhu Jiner notched up her first victory of the tournament, beating Kateryna Lagno in 44 moves; Alexandra Kosteniuk pounced on an error from Nino Batsiashvili to score another four points, while Pranav Venkatesh forced Abhimanyu Mishra’s resignation on the Prodigy board. With the Continental Kings picking 12 points for three victories with black pieces, Arjun Erigaisi’s win over Wei Yi and 15-year-old Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus beating Aravindh Chithambaram did not really help the Alaskan Knights chances of making it to the final. Alpine APL Pipers vs. Fyers American Gambits: 9-7 Pipers and American Gambits were tied on match points and game points going into the round, and winning the match was equally important for both teams. World no. 1 Magnus Carlsen ended Candidates 2026 winner Javokhir Sindarov’s three-game winning streak, and Vidit Gujrathi defeated Daniil Dubov in a rook-knight endgame to help defending champions Alpine APL Pipers beat FYERS American Gambits 9-7 in the clash of the top two teams. Carlsen, who won the Player of the Match award, was in total control throughout against Sindarov on the icon board and forced the Uzbek player to resign after 36 moves. “First of all, I think this was a great match with a very good team performance. We are thrilled to get the win. In my game, I was doing pretty well early on but he (Sindarov) put up a big fight, but I was able to wriggle out and find the win,” said Carlsen, who said Vidit deserved the trophy more than him and then handed the trophy to the Indian GM. The game between Vidit and Dubov on the Superstar men board went into a time scramble, but the Indian GM kept his cool as he made the most of his opportunities in an equal endgame to claim victory after a marathon 96-move battle and help Pipers complete a double over the Gambits. “It was a very close match, and when I saw the board, we were not in a clear position to win. I felt that I played a good game, and it was very good to win for the team,” said Vidit. Women’s World Cup winner Divya Deshmukh’s struggles in her debut GCL continued as she ran out of time on move 34 against Bibisara Assaubayeva for the only loss for her team on Friday. Ganges Grandmasters vs. CheQ Mumba Masters: 16-1 Ganges Grandmasters’ icon player Ian Nepomniachtchi, Superstar men Levon Aronian and Leinier Dominguez Perez, Superstar women Stavroula Tsolakidou and prodigy Leon Luke Mendonca made the most of the opportunity of playing white as they recorded convincing wins over their respective opponents. Only Polina Shuvalova drew her game against Harika Dronavalli to hand one point to the Mumba Masters. Standings after Day 7 Schedule for Saturday, September 12: 5.00 PM: Triveni Continental Kings vs. Alpine APL Pipers6.30 PM: PBG Alaskan Knights vs. Ganges Grandmasters8.00 PM: FYERS American Gambits vs. CheQ Mumba Masters About the Global Chess League The Global Chess League (GCL), a joint initiative between Tech Mahindra and FIDE, is the world’s first and largest official franchise league of its kind. The league brings together leading chess players from across the globe in a unique joint team format, with six players representing each franchise across Icons, Superstar Men, Superstar Women, and Prodigies. Men and women compete together on the same team, with every board carrying equal value towards the team’s result. GCL has previously staged seasons in Dubai, London, and Mumbai and returns to India for Season 4 in Bengaluru. GCL official website: https://globalchessleague.com/

title: A universal language: Chess, inclusion and friendship take center stage in Samarkand
summary: The first moves have been played at the 3rd FIDE Chess Olympiad for People with Disabilities, with 41 teams beginning their campaigns in Samarkand. Following Thursday’s opening ceremony, Round 1 brought the focus to the chessboards. Most of the favourites started confidently, but the opening day also produced some early surprises. Beyond the results, conversations with players from around the world highlighted what lies at the heart of the event: inclusion, equality, friendship and a shared love of chess. The ceremonial first move was made by Akaki Iashvili, FIDE Special Tasks Director and FIDE Technical Delegate of the Olympiad for People with Disabilities, and Komil Sindarov, Vice President of the Uzbekistan Chess Federation, on Board 1 of the Poland – Mongolia match. The encounter proved to be one of the closest of the opening round. Poland won on the top two boards, while Mongolia struck back on Boards 3 and 4 to secure a 2–2 draw. Favourites start strongly, but surprises come early Most of the higher-rated teams successfully navigated their opening matches. Cuba defeated IPCA 3½–½, Israel overcame Bangladesh by the same score, while Germany, USA, Ukraine and Hungary all began with perfect 4–0 victories.  The Philippines made an impressive start with a 3½–½ victory over Brazil. Argentina defeated Egypt 3–1, the Czech Republic beat Belarus 3–1, India overcame Uzbekistan 2 by the same score, Serbia defeated Vietnam 3–1, Switzerland beat Zimbabwe 3–1, Kazakhstan defeated ICCD 3–1, and Spain recorded a 3½–½ victory over China. Uzbekistan 1 gave the home supporters plenty to celebrate with a 4–0 victory against Uganda. But not everything went according to rating. One of the biggest surprises came from Kyrgyzstan, who defeated the considerably higher-rated Turkmenistan team 3–1. After draws on the first two boards, Toktobek Bolotov and Gulzat Kasymbaeva delivered victories on Boards 3 and 4 to seal the match. There was another home success for Uzbekistan 3, who defeated higher-rated Venezuela 2½–1½. Ali Irgashev drew on the top board, while Abdurahmon Azimjonov and Abbas Eshmuratov scored the two victories for the Uzbek team. Croatia and Türkiye also shared the points in a 2–2 draw. “This can become a tradition” For Komil Sindarov, Vice President of the Uzbekistan Chess Federation, bringing the Olympiad for People with Disabilities together with the main Chess Olympiad in the same host city represents something bigger than the competition itself. “This is the first time here in Uzbekistan that the Olympiad for People with Disabilities and the Olympiad are being held at the same time. Of course, this also brings certain organizational challenges. But I believe that we must protect the rights of people with disabilities and respect them,” he said (translated from Uzbek). “We believe that the foundation being laid here in Uzbekistan today will help make it possible for the Olympiad for People with Disabilities and the Olympiad to be held at the same time in the future. I believe that this tradition will continue” (translated from Uzbek). Sindarov said that seeing the joy of participants who had travelled to Samarkand from around the world had made a particular impression on him. “When I see the happiness on their faces, I feel very happy myself. People with disabilities, who may sometimes feel that some of their opportunities are limited, can today stand equally alongside everyone else, alongside other chess players, and participate in an Olympiad like this.” (translated from Uzbek). He also reflected on the rapid development of chess in Uzbekistan, pointing to improved coaching opportunities, scholarships, training camps and the country’s growing international tournament calendar. “Whereas we once had only one or two tournaments, today we have 24 international tournaments a year. We are creating all the necessary conditions for our chess players to compete and improve their level.” (translated from Uzbek). A perfect start for the hosts Uzbekistan 1 began its campaign with a clean sweep against Uganda, winning 4–0. On the top board, Axadxon Kimsanboyev defeated Enock Seguya with the black pieces. After the game, Kimsanboyev explained that after the queens were exchanged, he felt he had obtained a favourable endgame and eventually converted his advantage. “This game was not easy for me, but I’m expecting very hard games against the top players,” he said. Having participated in every edition of the Olympiad, Kimsanboyev has watched the competition grow first-hand. “The first Olympiad was in Belgrade in 2023, and the second Olympiad was in 2025. At the first Olympiad, I took a silver medal on Board 4. Every Olympiad, the number of participants is getting bigger and bigger. I hope that in the next Olympiad even more teams will participate, and we will meet more friends at the chessboard.” His own chess journey began at the age of ten, when his grandfather taught him the game. International competition followed from 2021, and chess gradually became one of the defining parts of his life. “Chess is one of the most important things in my life. Chess has helped me find more friends, win medals, participate in more competitions, and travel to more countries.” Chess as inclusion and equality For Gweshe Shantel of Zimbabwe, the opening round brought a difficult game but also the beginning of another important international experience. “The first game was a bit tough for me, but I’m hoping that for the next games I’m going to make it,” she said. Shantel has competed in university chess tournaments and recently took part in the Minerva tournament in Harare as part of her preparation for Samarkand. She also spoke about how participating internationally has changed her ambitions as a player. “The first time when I came, I didn’t have any rating, and now I have a rating that needs to be maintained. I also want to continue participating in other tournaments, even women’s tournaments, national tournaments and international tournaments.” Her relationship with chess began much earlier, at the age of six, through her father. “My dad was a chess player. title: FIDE World U7-U17 Rapid and Blitz Championships 2026 Egypt: Registration now open
summary: The International Chess Federation (FIDE) and the Egyptian Chess Federation are pleased to announce the 2026 FIDE World U7-U17 Rapid and Blitz Championships. The event will take place in Cairo, Egypt, from December 8 (arrival) to December 15 (departure), 2026. The participants will compete across six age categories: Under 7, Under 9, Under 11, Under 13, Under 15, and Under 17, with separate Open and Girls sections. Players who secured first place in the previous edition of the FIDE World Rapid & Blitz Cadets & Youth Championships (U9–U17 age groups) are granted the personal right to participate in the corresponding (or higher) age category, provided they meet the age requirement as of January 1, 2026. FIDE Member Federations may register any number of players and accompanying officials/persons. The registration deadline is November 1, 2026. Invitation, regulations, schedule (PDF) Registration details Registration form: https://forms.gle/sJW3H1QfS5FZ3kqE8 Email: youthrapidblitz@fide.com  Official website: https://youthrapidblitz2026.fide.com
